subject: Business
title: Marketplace Business Models
description: A micro-lesson that makes Marketplace Business Models usable.

hook.text: Uber owns no cars. Airbnb owns no apartments. Yet they're worth more than traditional rivals.

buildup.text: A marketplace connects supply and demand and takes a cut of each transaction.

discovery.text: The chicken-and-egg problem is the hardest: buyers need sellers and sellers need buyers.

twist.text: Most marketplaces subsidize one side first. Uber gave free rides to build the rider base.

climax.text: Once both sides are locked in, switching costs keep them there. That's the real moat.

punchline.text: Own the connection, not the inventory.

quiz.question: What is the biggest challenge for a new marketplace?
options: The chicken-and-egg problem of attracting both sides

details.summary: Marketplace startups connect buyers and sellers, earning revenue from transactions without owning inventory. The chicken-and-egg challenge of attracting both sides simultaneously is the central obstacle, while network effects create powerful defensibility once critical mass is achieved.

faq.question: How do successful marketplaces solve the chicken-and-egg problem?
faq.answer: Constrain to a single geographic or category niche to achieve density. Subsidize one side to attract the other. Create value for one side independent of the other. Manually recruit initial supply. Uber started in one city with a small number of drivers subsidized by high pay.

faq.question: What metrics matter most for marketplace businesses?
faq.answer: Gross merchandise volume measures total transactions. Take rate is the percentage captured as revenue. Liquidity measures how reliably buyers find sellers and vice versa. Repeat usage indicates marketplace stickiness. Supply utilization shows whether supply is being effectively matched with demand.
